deities: Maa Majhighariani (fierce form of Shakti/Durga; also called Majhi Gouri; worshipped mainly as a vermilion-smeared face; the horse is her mount per local belief)
festivals: Chaitra Parva (March–April); Sundays, Wednesdays and Fridays draw heavy crowds

history.period: Original 16th century (one source says 14th century — flagged); present structure late 20th century
history.summary: The principal Shakti shrine of Rayagada, on the Nagavali river in Rayagada town. Per the Odisha District Gazetteer, the 16th-century Suryavanshi king Vishwanath Dev Gajapati moved his capital from Nandapur to Rayagada, built a fort on the Nagavali (later demolished by the British, who reused its stones for a bridge) and installed the goddess in the central room of his palace — hence 'Majhi Ghariani', 'she who dwells in the central room'. The present Kalinga-style temple is only about 40 years old (built late 20th century) on/near the old site. Legend holds the king brought the idol from Jeypore; she protected him in battle as he expanded his kingdom. Famous far beyond Odisha — devotees come from Andhra Pradesh and Chhattisgarh; the goddess is described as fiery and smeared in red vermilion, and goats/chicken are offered per visitor accounts. Note: one travel source (Tripadvisor-derived) claims a 14th-century origin and a railway-bridge miracle legend; the gazetteer-based account (16th century) is preferred but both are flagged.

name: Majhighariani Temple
town_description: Rayagada is a town in southern Odisha on the Nagavali river and the headquarters of Rayagada district — a major railway junction on the Raipur–Visakhapatnam line and the commercial hub of the tribal KBK region, ringed by Eastern Ghats hill ranges.

travel.airport: Visakhapatnam (~210 km), Raipur or Bhubaneswar — nearest major airports
travel.railway: Rayagada Junction (town station, on the Raipur–Visakhapatnam line)
travel.road: Beside the railway track in Rayagada town, on Chilakapalem Parvathipuram Road; well connected by state buses

visitor_information.best_time: October (Dussehra) and March–April (Chaitra Parva); October–March generally
